references.text: God's promise to Abraham that he would become the father of many nations and that kings would come from him, which is reflected in the prophecy that Ephraim's descendants would become a multitude of nations (melo ha-goyim).
God renews the promise to Jacob about a nation and a gathering of nations coming from him, a direct parallel to the promise that Ephraim's descendants would become 'a multitude of nations.'
Jacob crosses his hands and places his right hand on Ephraim's head, even though he is the younger one—the background for Jacob's words that the younger brother will become greater than the older.
Jacob's blessings over Joseph and his descendants, with prophecies about their future greatness and blessings, parallel to the blessing given to Ephraim and Manasseh.

At the census, the tribe of Ephraim numbered 40,500 men, while the tribe of Manasseh counted 32,200 (vv. 34–35), showing the fulfillment of Jacob's prophecy that Ephraim would become greater than Manasseh.

Moses' blessing over Joseph's tribe, which includes both Ephraim and Manasseh, and predicts their greatness. Verse 17 explicitly mentions Ephraim's ten thousands and Manasseh's thousands, in line with Jacob's prophecy.

Paul explains that the Gentiles are co-heirs and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus, which can be seen as a fulfillment of the promise that Abraham's and Jacob's descendants would become 'a multitude of nations.'
Paul confirms that Jacob's prophecy about a lineage consisting of many peoples is a central promise now being fulfilled through faith.
Both texts illustrate the principle that God chooses the younger brother to carry the blessing or power rather than the older.
